name: Turkey illusion
statement: The turkey illusion is the error of treating a situation of uncertainty as one of calculable risk, so confidence peaks just before the break.
meaning: Gerd Gigerenzer states the target plainly in his 2020 handbook chapter: 'Many psychologists do not distinguish between risk and uncertainty but instead believe that all problems can be solved by probability theory, as assumed in Bayesian theories of mind or brain. This position has been criticized as being the "turkey illusion."' The distinction he draws is Frank Knight's, whose 1921 book the chapter cites. Under risk the outcomes and their probabilities are known, and calculation suffices. Under uncertainty the set of outcomes is not known, and surprises happen. In the parable the turkey updates on the only two outcomes it can imagine, fed or not fed, and by Bayesian updating its confidence is highest on day 100. That day is the one before Thanksgiving. Gigerenzer's own gloss is that the turkey 'missed a crucial piece of information: It was not in a situation of risk, where the past predicts the future.' He applies the charge to institutions rather than to birds, writing that it 'appears to be committed more frequently by humans than turkeys'. The illusion is a criticism of how uncertainty is modelled, not a claim about a measurable tendency in individuals.

origin.note: No source claiming to have coined the phrase was located. The earliest dated use found is the German form, Truthahn-Illusion, in Der Spiegel of 17 March 2013. The standfirst of the interview 'Winchester unterm Christbaum' says Gigerenzer warns of the traps of the 'Truthahn-Illusion'. The next dated use found is the headline of an interview with him by Heike Littger in managerSeminare, issue 182, of May 2013, which opens at page 48. Both accompanied his book 'Risiko: Wie man die richtigen Entscheidungen trifft', which the German National Library catalogue records as Munich, Bertelsmann, 2013, 396 pages, translated from the English by Hainer Kober. The English text appeared in 2014 as 'Risk Savvy: How to Make Good Decisions', whose chapter 2, 'Certainty Is an Illusion', begins at page 17. Neither book's text was obtained, so this entry does not claim the phrase appears in either, and the German edition's table of contents names no chapter for the turkey. Gigerenzer uses the term in print in the 2020 chapter cited below and again in 2025, and in neither place does he claim it as his own.

evidence: No experiment on the turkey illusion was located. Gigerenzer presents it as the third of three criticisms of choice axioms, alongside a descriptive and a prescriptive objection, and offers no data for it. Its support in the section at page 586 is the worked parable and one historical case. He writes of 'the increasing confidence of financial institutions in the stability of the financial market in the years before the crisis of 2007-2008, up to shortly before the breakdown', and adds that the rating agencies calibrated their models on the past years and predicted that the future resembles the past. No figure, dataset or named agency accompanies that claim. Taleb's Las Vegas casino belongs to the chapter's opening pages on risk and uncertainty, six pages earlier, and not to the turkey section. There Gigerenzer writes that the owner could calculate the gambling odds, yet 'the main losses occurred through unforeseeable events': a tiger attacking the star artist, a disgruntled former contractor attempting to dynamite the casino, and an employee who failed to file tax reports for a long period. He cites Taleb 2007, pages 129 to 130. Taleb's own account of that casino is longer than the paraphrase, and entry 177 sets it out from the book. The measured work the chapter attaches to the risk and uncertainty distinction sits one step away from the illusion. It reports that Ellsberg showed people's preferences over gambles to be sensitive to whether the probabilities are known or ambiguous. Ellsberg's paper was read for this entry, and it rests on the considered choices of colleagues and other individuals rather than on a controlled experiment. He concludes at page 669 that for such people the Bayesian or Savage approach 'gives wrong predictions and, by their lights, bad advice'. The chapter also lists the 1/N rule, allocating resources equally across N alternatives, with the note that it can outperform optimal asset allocation portfolios, citing DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal. That paper was not obtained for this entry.

examples.tag: The charity that budgets from its own history
examples.text: A small charity has five steady years of donations and sets next year's budget as a narrow band around them. The band is calculated from a stretch in which nothing changed, and it carries no line for the grant programme closing. Confidence in the figure is highest the week before the letter arrives.

examples.tag: The supplier that has never failed
examples.text: A team estimates the chance of a supply failure from a log in which the supplier never failed, so the estimate tightens with every quiet quarter. What the log cannot hold is the outcome it has no row for, and the tightest number is the one printed last.

A landlord who has been paid on the first of the month for eight years writes the rent into next year's figures as settled. The record supports a probability, and the situation it was drawn from is one where the outcomes were never the only two on offer.

replication.headline: No replication attempt was found, because there is no original study to repeat. The turkey illusion is a name for a way of modelling badly, and nobody appears to have turned it into a claim about people that could pass or fail.
replication.detail: Crossref, Europe PMC and arXiv were searched on 21 September 2026 for the English and the German phrase, and none returns a study carrying it. Crossref holds 'The Blind Turkey', of 2025, which is about observer ignorance and black swans rather than about this label. Gigerenzer's own chapter cites no study for the illusion and reports no data, and his 2025 article in Behavioural Public Policy repeats the label in one sentence and reports none either. The nearest measured relative is ambiguity aversion, and it is a different claim. Ambiguity aversion concerns known against vague probabilities over a fixed set of outcomes, while the turkey illusion concerns a set of outcomes the decision maker never imagined. Counting work on the first as a test of the second would be the error the entry warns about.

limits: The search for a study was run on 21 September 2026 and covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic query, Europe PMC for both the English and the German phrase, arXiv, and general web search. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and CORE each answered 429 as rate-limited that day, BASE refused this network by address, and the Google Books API answered 429 for want of daily quota, so those five indexes went unsearched. Neither 'Risk Savvy' nor 'Risiko' was obtained. The Internet Archive holds a lending-restricted scan of the former, and its search-inside route answered HTTP 403 with 'Item not available' rather than an error. This entry therefore cannot say on which page, or in which of the two books, the phrase first reached print, and its 2013 date rests on two magazine texts rather than on the book. The body of the Der Spiegel interview sits behind the SPIEGEL+ metered paywall, so only its headline, standfirst and date were read. Of the managerSeminare interview, pages 48 and 49 were read as the excerpt the German Wikipedia article links, and that excerpt carries no byline. One further item named by that article was not obtained: a 2014 blog account of a Gigerenzer talk, whose address now redirects to a different site, and whose archived copy this session's egress policy refuses. The 2020 chapter was read in a full-text copy of the handbook's second edition posted at dokumen.pub rather than at Cambridge, and the turkey passage was fetched twice with identical wording. Chalmers was read in the third edition of 1999; earlier editions were not checked.
misreadings: The story is credited to Russell, and Russell wrote about a chicken. Chapter VI of his 'The Problems of Philosophy' of 1912 says that 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.' There is no turkey, no nine o'clock feeding, no Christmas and no named illusion. The turkey arrives with Alan Chalmers, whose 'What Is This Thing Called Science?' gives at page 45 of the third edition 'a somewhat gruesome example attributed to Bertrand Russell' about a bird fed at 9 am whose throat is cut on Christmas eve. Chalmers writes 'attributed to', and the term inductivist turkey appears nowhere in the text of that edition as searched for this entry. The credit hardens anyway. Kováč's 2013 note in EMBO Reports calls it the famous parable of Bertrand Russell's inductivist turkey, the German Wikipedia article cites that note for the claim that Russell described the bias, and the English article repeats the claim. The English article cites Gigerenzer for it, and Gigerenzer says the opposite in the same sentence: the illusion 'goes back to the philosopher Bertrand Russell (who used a chicken in his account), and has been popularized by trader Nassim Taleb'. Taleb is the second stop and is the more careful of the two. His footnote to chapter 4 of 'The Black Swan' reads 'Since Russell's original example used a chicken, this is the enhanced North American adaptation.' The phrase turkey illusion does not occur in the scanned text of that book searched for this entry. Gigerenzer's later use points the same way. In 2025 he writes that applying Bayes' rule to an uncertain world of sudden change can lead to the 'turkey illusion', and cites Taleb 2010 for it. The last error is to file the illusion with the cognitive biases and expect an effect size. Gigerenzer aims it at psychologists who model uncertainty as risk, and at rating agencies, not at a tendency measured in individuals.

sources.text: Gigerenzer, G. (2020). Intelligence and Decision-Making. In R. J. Sternberg (Ed.), The Cambridge Handbook of Intelligence, 2nd ed. (pp. 580-601). Cambridge University Press. The section 'The Turkey Illusion' is at page 586, as the volume's index confirms, and the casino example is in the chapter's opening pages. Read as the full text of the second edition posted at dokumen.pub; the passage was fetched twice and matched.

Littger, H. (2013). Gerd Gigerenzer über Risikointelligenz: 'Die Truthahn-Illusion leitet uns fehl'. managerSeminare, issue 182, May 2013. The headline, author, issue and date were read at the publisher's article page. Pages 48 and 49 were read as the excerpt linked below, in which the phrase carries the headline and the preview rather than any answer Gigerenzer gives.

Deutsche Nationalbibliothek catalogue record for Gigerenzer, G. (2013). Risiko: Wie man die richtigen Entscheidungen trifft. Munich: Bertelsmann, 396 pages, ISBN 978-3-570-10103-2, 'Aus dem Engl. von Hainer Kober'. Source for the German edition's publisher, year and translation.

Table of contents of Gigerenzer, G., Risk Savvy: How to Make Good Decisions, Penguin Books edition, ISBN 978-0-241-95461-4, scanned by the ETH Zurich library. Source for the chapter titles and opening pages quoted here, including chapter 2, 'Certainty Is an Illusion', at page 17. The body text of the book was not obtained.
Russell, B. (1912). The Problems of Philosophy. Chapter VI, 'On Induction', supplies the chicken passage. Read as the Project Gutenberg plain text, ebook 5827.

Chalmers, A. F. (1999). What Is This Thing Called Science? Third edition, Hackett Publishing Company, reprinted from the University of Queensland Press third edition. The turkey passage is at page 45, in chapter 4, 'Deriving theories from the facts: induction'. Read as a scanned PDF with a text layer.

Taleb, N. N. (2007). The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable. Chapter 4, 'One Thousand and One Days, or How Not to Be a Sucker', and its endnote on Russell's chicken. Read as the full text at the Internet Archive, an open upload rather than a lending copy, and searched there on 21 September 2026. Entry 177 reads the same scan for the casino passage.

Kováč, L. (2013). Homo artefaciens. EMBO Reports, 14(6), 482. Full text read at the PubMed Central page for PMC3674451 on 21 September 2026, the Europe PMC XML route having answered HTTP 500 that day. It calls the story 'the famous parable of Bertrand Russell's "inductivist turkey"'. The source the German Wikipedia article cites for attributing the parable to Russell.

Littger, H. (2013). 'Die Truthahn-Illusion leitet uns fehl'. managerSeminare, issue 182, May 2013, pages 48 to 49. The excerpt linked from the German Wikipedia article, read as a PDF. Source for the teaser, which says turkeys reckon that yesterday's feeding predicts tomorrow's, a reckoning that knows nothing of Thanksgiving.

Der Spiegel (2013). SPIEGEL-GESPRÄCH: 'Winchester unterm Christbaum'. Der Spiegel 12/2013, published 17 March 2013. The standfirst says the Berlin psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer warns of the traps of the 'Truthahn-Illusion'. Headline, standfirst and date were read at the publisher's page; the body sits behind the SPIEGEL+ paywall.

Gigerenzer, G. (2025). The rationality wars: a personal reflection. Behavioural Public Policy, 9(3), 495-515. His own later use of the label, in one sentence and with no data, crediting Taleb 2010 for it. Full text read as the PDF at Cambridge Core.

Table of contents of Gigerenzer, G. (2013). Risiko: Wie man die richtigen Entscheidungen trifft, held by the German National Library. Twelve chapters, among them chapter 2, 'Gewissheit ist eine Illusion', at page 30, and none named for the turkey.

Wikipedia, 'Truthahn-Illusion' and 'Turkey illusion', wikitext read on 21 September 2026. Cited as the object of the attribution error described above, not as evidence for anything. The German article also links the two magazine texts used here.

Ellsberg, D. (1961). Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 75(4), 643-669. Cited by Gigerenzer's chapter for the ambiguity result described above. Read as the JSTOR scan posted at dklevine.com, the publisher's own page having answered HTTP 403.

DeMiguel, V., Garlappi, L., & Uppal, R. (2009). Optimal versus naive diversification: How inefficient is the 1/N portfolio strategy? Review of Financial Studies, 22(5), 1915-1953. Cited by Gigerenzer's chapter for the 1/N rule. Not obtained on 21 September 2026: the publisher and the SSRN record both answered HTTP 403, the London Business School record holds metadata and no file, and Unpaywall reports no open copy anywhere.
